sections.title: What these excerpts are about
sections.text: Stiny explains shape grammars through questions about definition, expressive scope, use and creative interpretation. The reviewed examples emphasize calculation as repeatedly seeing a part, changing it, and seeing the fused result afresh.

sections.title: The main premise
sections.text: A drawing need not retain the decomposition used to create it. The next rule can identify other parts, so a fixed symbolic inventory is not the sole available description. Even an identity rule can reveal a part or symmetry without changing the drawing.

sections.title: Method and worked example
sections.text: In Q1, a square rule adds an inscribed square: match a transformed left side and replace it using the same transformation on the right. Exhibit 2 follows triangle rotations through configurations read as three triangles, then two, then three again.

sections.title: What the example demonstrates
sections.text: A rule rotating a selected triangle about its own center can participate in a larger calculation whose original triangle centers move. There is no contradiction: the calculation reselects different triangles instead of tracking permanent objects through every step.

sections.title: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The examples are visual arguments, not participant experiments. In Q6, Stiny reports professional use but declines to identify projects, so that passage does not supply independently checkable adoption evidence. No universal claim about all software follows from these examples.

sections.title: How to read and experiment
sections.text: Try an identity rule first to mark alternative parts, then a changing rule. After each step, ask what can be seen now rather than only what was drawn before. Keep this course-hosted manuscript distinct from the final 2022 publication.
